newsitem.title: USA: Clinton "quite optimistic" on chemical treaty.
newsitem.headline: Clinton "quite optimistic" on chemical treaty.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Tuesday he was "quite optimistic" the Senate would approve a treaty outlawing chemical weapons this week.

"We've worked very hard on this and I'm actually quite optimistic," Clinton told reporters at the White House on the eve of Senate debate on the Chemical Weapons Convention. Later he won the support of a key Republican when Sen. Alfonse D'Amato of New York announced he would support the treaty.

"I believe the chemical weapons treaty is the most effective mechanism we have to ensure that these weapons of horror are not used against citizens of the United States and the world," D'Amato said in a statement.

Clinton has mounted an intensive lobbying effort to win the necessary two-thirds Senate majority to ratify the treaty in the face of conservative opposition. He wants the Senate to strip out four "killer" amendments before Thursday's vote.

Agreement has been reached on 28 other amendments to clarify treaty provisions without torpedoing U.S. participation in the pact, which goes into effect on April 29, with or without the United States.

The treaty needs 67 votes if all senators vote. Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle last week put the chances of approval at no better than 50-50, but top administration officials have joined Clinton in keeping up the pressure for approval of the treaty.

"I worked over the weekend some on it," Clinton said. "We're doing the best we can to put together a strong case and the fact that we have come up with a package of 28 clarifying amendments that respond to 90 percent of the objections of even the strongest opponents of the treaty. ... It shows the good faith in which we have proceeded."

The "killer" amendments include raising the standards of verification against cheating to what experts consider unachievable levels, linking U.S. participation to Russian ratification of the pact and insisting that countries alleged to support international terrorism such as Iraq and Libya join before the United States does.
